title: Do Air Purifiers Actually Work?
h1: Do Air Purifiers Actually Work, and When Are They Worth It?
description: Air purifiers do work on dust, pollen, pet dander and smoke when they're sized right and use a true HEPA filter. Here's what they can and can't fix at home.
quick_answer: Yes, a good air purifier works on airborne particles like dust, pollen, pet dander and wildfire smoke, as long as it uses a true HEPA filter and is sized for the room. It won't fix moisture, mold growth or dirt that's already settled, and it only cleans the air that passes through it. Think of it as one tool, not a complete fix.
body:
Air purifiers do what they claim for particles in the air, but they're often bought for problems they can't solve. A HEPA purifier sized for the room will pull dust, pollen, pet dander and smoke out of the air you're breathing. It won't stop a damp crawl space from smelling musty or remove the dust sitting in your carpet.

What do air purifiers remove from the air?

A unit with a true HEPA filter is good at capturing fine particles, which covers most of what people care about:

  • Pollen during spring and fall allergy seasons
  • Pet dander and dust mite debris
  • Wildfire smoke particles during Santa Ana fire season
  • Fine dust from remodeling or nearby construction

Purifiers with an activated carbon filter can also reduce some odors and chemical fumes, such as cooking smells and vapors from paint or new furniture. How much depends on the amount of carbon. A thin carbon sheet doesn't do much.

What can't an air purifier fix?

This is where people end up disappointed. A purifier won't:

  • Stop mold that's growing on a wall, in a closet or in the attic
  • Lower humidity or dry out a damp space
  • Clean dust that has settled on floors, furniture and inside ducts
  • Remove carbon monoxide or a gas leak. Those need detectors and a call for help, not filtration.
  • Undo a constant source, like a leaky return duct pulling in attic air

If the problem has a source, deal with the source first. A purifier then handles what's left.

How do I know if an air purifier is the right size?

Look for the Clean Air Delivery Rate, or CADR, on the box. It tells you how much filtered air the unit puts out. Match it to the size of the room, and size up if you have high ceilings or want it to work quietly on a low setting.

A small unit in a big open living room will run all day and barely make a difference. Placement matters too. Put it where you spend the most time, often the bedroom, and keep it a little away from walls and furniture so air can move through it.

Is a portable purifier or a whole-home system better?

Portable units clean one room well. Whole-home options work through your HVAC system and treat the air every time the fan runs. They include high-efficiency media filters, electronic air cleaners and UV lights that target growth on the coil.

A whole-home setup makes sense if several people in the house have allergies, you want cleaner air in every room, or you deal with smoke every fire season. It only works while the fan runs, so many people set the fan to run more often during bad air days. Our indoor air quality team can tell you which options fit your system and ductwork.

Are there air purifiers I should avoid?

Be cautious with units that create ozone on purpose, sometimes sold as "ozone generators" or "activated oxygen." Ozone irritates the lungs, and California regulates indoor air cleaners for ozone output, so check that any unit you buy meets that standard.

Also skip models with filters described as "HEPA-type" or "HEPA-like" without a real rating. Those don't meet the same standard as true HEPA. And remember that any purifier is only as good as its filter. A clogged filter moves less air and cleans less.

What else improves indoor air besides a purifier?

A purifier works best as part of a simple routine. Change your HVAC filter on schedule, and use the highest-rated filter your system can handle without choking airflow. Run the bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans when you shower or cook so moisture and fumes leave the house.

Keep humidity in check, especially in coastal homes where the marine layer keeps things damp, because dust mites and mildew both like moisture. And have leaky return ducts sealed, since they can pull in attic or garage air that no portable unit can keep up with.
faqs: Do air purifiers help with allergies?

They can help with airborne allergens like pollen, pet dander and dust. Many people notice the biggest difference in the bedroom overnight. They work best alongside regular cleaning and a good filter in the HVAC system.
Should I run my air purifier all the time?

Running it continuously on a lower setting usually works better than short bursts on high. Particles keep entering the air from outside and from daily activity, so steady filtering keeps levels lower.
Do air purifiers help with wildfire smoke?
Yes. A HEPA purifier sized for the room is one of the most effective ways to reduce smoke particles indoors. Keep windows closed and consider a unit with a carbon filter for the smell.
How often do air purifier filters need changing?

It depends on the model and how dirty your air is. Many HEPA filters last several months to a year, and carbon filters often need changing sooner. Check the manufacturer's guidance, and change it early after heavy smoke.
